title: Decision trees, forests & boosting
summary: A practical family of models for structured data, nonlinear interactions, and strong baselines.
html:
A practical family of models for structured data, nonlinear interactions, and strong baselines.

Trees partition feature space

A decision tree chooses splits that make child nodes more homogeneous under an objective. Following splits routes a sample to a leaf with a prediction. Depth, minimum leaf size, and pruning limit complexity. Trees can model interactions without manually enumerating every feature combination.

Random forests reduce variance

A forest fits many trees using randomized samples and feature choices, then aggregates predictions. Diversity reduces correlated errors. More trees often stabilize predictions but increase memory and inference work. Out-of-bag estimates can be useful under their sampling assumptions; they do not replace an appropriate temporal or grouped holdout.

Boosting corrects residual mistakes

Gradient boosting adds weak learners sequentially to reduce an objective. Learning rate, tree count, leaf complexity, and subsampling control capacity. Early stopping uses a validation set. Modern implementations optimize histograms, missing-value handling, and hardware efficiency.

Interpretation requires care

Feature importance can favor high-cardinality variables or distribute credit unpredictably among correlated features. Permutation importance measures a change in predictive performance under a particular perturbation. Partial dependence can evaluate unrealistic combinations when features are correlated.

Worked example

MethodHow learners combineMain tradeoff
Single treeOne partitionReadable when small; unstable when deep
Random forestAverage randomized treesRobust baseline; larger model
Gradient boostingSequential corrective additionsStrong fit; careful tuning and leakage control

What goes wrong

Training deep trees until error vanishes invites overfitting. A feature that predicts well may be a leakage channel or a proxy, not a causal driver.

Check your understanding

Why does averaging identical trees give little benefit?

Reveal the explanation

Their errors are perfectly correlated. Ensembles gain from useful diversity, not just repeated copies.

How the pieces connect

A usable chapter has a flow of decisions, evidence, and checks. Use this diagram as a navigation aid, then test each step on a small real example.

An operating model for decision trees, forests & boosting

Trees are powerful because they create interactions and nonlinear regions without feature engineering, but every split is a chance to memorize an accident of the sample. Forests reduce variance through diverse trees; boosting reduces residual error through sequential trees. The choice depends on data size, noise, latency, and explainability needs.

The diagram is deliberately sequential, but real systems loop. A surprising result may expose a bad representation; a production incident may reveal a missing evaluation slice; a performance limit may require an algorithmic change. The point is to preserve the link between the abstract concept, the evidence you observe, and the decision you make next.

Field guide: four decisions in order

1. Partition

Partition establishes the next constraint. A tree selects feature conditions. Begin by making the object of study explicit. A vague input, target, or operating condition creates ambiguity that later computation cannot repair.

Write down the input boundary and the unit of analysis. This makes it possible to distinguish a missing fact from a mismatch between the question and the data or system.

2. Regularize

Regularize establishes the next constraint. Depth, leaves, and sampling control capacity. Now make the mechanism inspectable. Prefer a small run whose intermediate values, examples, or traces can be examined before you automate a larger workflow.

Keep a concrete artifact: a small dataset, a notebook cell, a trace, a benchmark command, or a hand-worked calculation. It is the fastest way to surface hidden assumptions.

3. Combine

Combine establishes the next constraint. Average or sequentially correct weak learners. Treat the first result as a measurement, not a conclusion. Compare it with a baseline and vary one assumption at a time so that the observed change has an interpretable cause.

Check a deliberately awkward case alongside the happy path. Boundary conditions, rare examples, and resource limits reveal more than another aggregate score.

4. Inspect

Inspect establishes the next constraint. Test importances and errors against leakage and proxies. Finish by connecting the result to a real choice. Record the operating range, uncertainty, and the condition under which the next person should stop, escalate, or revisit the earlier steps.

Preserve the decision record with the result. A useful technical chapter leaves enough context for a reader to reproduce the reasoning, challenge it, and choose a safe next action.

When the first approach fails

Do not respond to a weak result by immediately adding scale, complexity, or another framework. First locate the failure: the input may not match the intended problem; the representation may discard a useful signal; the measurement may reward the wrong outcome; or the system may have crossed a memory, latency, reliability, or authority boundary. Change one layer, repeat the smallest useful check, and keep the before-and-after evidence.

Gotcha. A polished output can hide an untested assumption. The most convincing demonstration is a counterexample the workflow handles deliberately, with the limitation stated in the release or research record.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. Partition. A tree selects feature conditions.
  2. Regularize. Depth, leaves, and sampling control capacity.
  3. Combine. Average or sequentially correct weak learners.
  4. Inspect. Test importances and errors against leakage and proxies.

Plot validation performance against depth or boosting rounds and use early stopping. Recompute feature attribution under perturbed data or alternate splits before treating it as an explanation.

Questions that keep the chapter honest

AskWhy it mattersEvidence to collect
What assumptions does this method make?Every method encodes a view of data, hardware, or behavior.Inputs, representations, constraints, and cases outside the expected range.
What would make the result fail?Failure modes show where an aggregate result is fragile.Boundary cases, counterexamples, slices, and perturbations.
What decision changes if it improves?A metric only matters through an operational action.Baseline, threshold, cost, latency, and human-review consequences.
